_meta.description: Single source of truth for the Basileian Canon intertextual + history-of-religions apparatus. Generates both the printed 'Index of Citations, Allusions & Traditions' and the reader-app marginal cross-references.
_meta.id_scheme: Frozen pericope IDs: Part.subsection (Roman part, e.g. I.1). Prologue = P. Reference IDs append a letter: I.1-a.

P.canon_title: The boy Jesus in the temple

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Greco-Roman 'boyhood-deeds-of-the-great-man' topos (paidika); Jewish wonder-child (young Samuel 1 Sam 2-3; Josephus on young Moses, Ant. 2.230; Philo, Mos. 1.21)
references.note: Ancient lives of significant figures routinely carried a single boyhood episode foreshadowing future greatness; the wonder-child was standard packaging. DIVERGENCE: Luke invokes the convention but deflates it. The boy performs no prodigy; he is found listening and asking questions of the teachers. Contrast the Infancy Gospel of Thomas, which takes the same convention and inflates it into a miracle-working (and lethal) child. Luke signals status through Torah-engagement, not magic. The restraint is the point.
scholarship: on the topos: Bultmann, History of the Synoptic Tradition, 300-301

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Temple-as-house-of-God (Ps 26:8; 1 Kgs 8; cf. Mal 3:1 LORD coming to his temple)
references.note: Jesus's first recorded words: 'in the [things/house] of my Father' (en tois tou patros mou) -- the phrase is elliptical and can mean 'house' or 'affairs/business.' First occurrence of the filial Father-language. The Temple-as-Father's-house resonance is real but the echo is faint and not marked as citation; rendered possible, not asserted.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: lost-and-found / 'after three days' motif
references.note: Frequently read as a resurrection-foreshadowing ('after three days they found him'). NOTED-AND-DISCOUNTED: the three-day interval here is most naturally the travel arithmetic (a day out, a day back, plus the searching), and Luke draws no resurrection inference. Included so the reader who has heard the typological reading sees it weighed and set aside rather than silently omitted.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Malachi 3:1 conflated with Exodus 23:20
references.note: Mark opens with a composite citation he attributes to 'Isaiah the prophet,' but the first half is not Isaiah: 'Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way' fuses Exodus 23:20 LXX (idou egO apostellO ton angelon mou) with Malachi 3:1. The mis-attribution is a known crux: some manuscripts 'correct' it to 'in the prophets.' Matthew and Luke remove the Malachi half from John's introduction and relocate it onto JESUS'S lips later (Matt 11:10 // Luke 7:27) -- a redactional tidy-up that exposes Mark as the earlier, rougher text. TEXT-FORM: blended, matching neither LXX cleanly.
scholarship: Metzger, Textual Commentary, on Mark 1:2 (the 'Isaiah'/'prophets' variant)

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Isaiah 40:3
references.note: 'A voice crying in the wilderness: prepare the way of YHWH' = Isaiah 40:3 LXX. The citation turns on a punctuation difference between Hebrew and Greek: MT reads 'a voice cries: in the wilderness prepare the way' (wilderness = location of the road); LXX/NT reads 'a voice crying in the wilderness: prepare' (wilderness = location of the crier). The Gospel needs the LXX division to make John, in the desert, the voice. ZEITGEIST: the same verse was the self-defining charter text of the Qumran community, which cited Isa 40:3 (1QS 8:13-14) to justify its literal withdrawal into the desert 'to prepare the way.' So a wilderness-renewal movement reading itself into Isa 40:3 was already a live first-century move -- John is doing independently what the yahad did. (Anarthrous Kyrios in LXX citation -> YHWH per the divine-names policy.)
scholarship: Marcus, AYB Mark, on 1:3 and 'The Way' in Mark
Brooke, The Dead Sea Scrolls and the New Testament, ch. on Isaiah 40

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Elijah typology: 2 Kings 1:8 (clothing); Malachi 4:5-6 [MT 3:23-24] (returning Elijah)
references.note: John's camel-hair garment and leather belt deliberately costume him as Elijah: 2 Kings 1:8 describes Elijah as 'a hairy man with a leather belt around his waist.' Combined with the messenger of Mal 3:1 (I.1-a), this casts John as the returning Elijah of Mal 4:5-6 who precedes the Day of YHWH. Mark makes the identification by wardrobe rather than statement; Matthew makes it explicit (Matt 11:14, 17:13).
scholarship: Ohler, 'The Expectation of Elijah and the Presence of the Kingdom of God,' JBL 118 (1999)

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Second Temple repentance-immersion / wilderness-prophet milieu; Josephus, Ant. 18.116-119
references.note: John's repentance-baptism belongs to a recognizable Second Temple landscape of immersion and purification movements. Josephus independently attests John as a popular figure executed by Antipas (Ant. 18.116-119) -- a control external to the Gospels, anchoring the historical John apart from his Christian framing as forerunner. The relation to Qumran's daily lustrations is a milieu-resemblance, not a borrowing: their immersions were repeated ritual purity, John's a once-for-all eschatological act. Direction flagged as shared milieu, not dependence.
scholarship: Meier, A Marginal Jew, vol. 2, on John

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: prophetic-commissioning theophany (Ezek 1:1 'heavens opened'; Isa 6); the bat qol (heavenly voice) convention
references.note: Opened heavens + Spirit + heavenly voice is the furniture of the prophetic call/commissioning scene (Ezekiel's 'the heavens were opened and I saw visions of God,' Ezek 1:1). The heavenly voice is the bat qol ('daughter of a voice'), the Second Temple and rabbinic substitute for prophecy after the prophets ceased. DIVERGENCE: a bat qol normally confirms or identifies; here it declares sonship and election, exceeding the convention. Mark also writes the heavens 'torn' (schizO), not merely opened -- a violent verb he reuses only at 15:38 (the veil), bracketing the Gospel.
scholarship: Marcus, AYB Mark, on the 'tearing' inclusio
on bat qol: Str-B I.125-134 (with dating caution)

references.speaker: other
references.source: Psalm 2:7 + Isaiah 42:1; agapEtos possibly evoking Genesis 22:2
references.note: The voice from heaven fuses three streams. 'You are my son' = Psalm 2:7 (royal-enthronement decree, LXX). 'in whom I am well pleased' = Isaiah 42:1 (the chosen Servant 'in whom my soul delights') -- but in a non-LXX form (LXX Isa 42:1 reads differently), suggesting a Hebraizing or testimony-source rendering. 'the beloved' (agapEtos) may additionally evoke Genesis 22:2, Isaac the 'beloved/only son' of the Aqedah. Royal Son + suffering Servant + bound Son, compressed into one sentence. The Servant strand is what loads the sonship with a trajectory toward the cross. CONFIDENCE: established for Ps 2 and Isa 42; the Gen 22 echo is probable and debated.
scholarship: Marcus, AYB Mark, on 1:11 and 'Son of God' / Servant fusion
Marcus, The Way of the Lord, 48-79

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: the dove (contested): Gen 1:2 LXX (Spirit hovering over the waters); Gen 8:8-12 (Noah's dove); Israel-as-dove (Hos 7:11)
references.note: The Spirit 'as a dove' is the famous undecidable. The strongest candidates are all available in the zeitgeist: (i) Genesis 1:2, the Spirit brooding over the primal waters -- new-creation at the water (b. Hagigah 15a likens the brooding Spirit to a dove); (ii) Genesis 8, Noah's dove returning over the receded flood -- new world after water; (iii) Israel figured as a dove (Hos 7:11; later rabbinic). No single decoding is secure, and the Gospels offer none. Left as possible, with the candidate set given rather than one source chosen -- this is a place not to resolve.
scholarship: Marcus, AYB Mark, on 1:10 (survey of dove interpretations)
Keener, The Gospel of Matthew, on 3:16

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: alleged pagan baptism/divine-sonship parallels (Mandaean; mystery-cult)
references.note: NOTED-AND-DISCOUNTED. The history-of-religions school once derived the baptism from Mandaean and mystery-cult initiation. This fails the availability gate: the Mandaean sources are centuries later and the direction of any contact is contested; the scene is saturated instead with Jewish scriptural material (Ps 2, Isa 42, Ezek 1, the bat qol). Recorded here so the comparison is seen to have been weighed and rejected on dating and provenance, not ignored.
scholarship: J. Z. Smith, Drudgery Divine (on the parallelomania hazard)

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: wilderness-testing + forty: Deut 8:2-3 (Israel 40 years); Exod 34:28 (Moses 40 days); 1 Kgs 19:8 (Elijah 40 days)
references.note: Forty days in the wilderness, tested, recapitulates Israel's forty years of testing (Deut 8:2-3), with secondary resonance of Moses's forty days on Sinai and Elijah's forty-day journey to Horeb. Jesus is cast as Israel re-run -- and, unlike Israel, passing the test. The Q version (I.3-b) makes the Israel-typology explicit by drawing all three replies from Deuteronomy's wilderness section.
scholarship: Gerhardsson, The Testing of God's Son

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Deuteronomy 8:3; Deuteronomy 6:16; Deuteronomy 6:13
references.note: Jesus answers each temptation with Deuteronomy, all from the wilderness-testing material: Deut 8:3 ('not by bread alone, but by every word from God's mouth'), Deut 6:16 ('you shall not test YHWH your God'), Deut 6:13 ('YHWH your God you shall worship, and him only serve'). Quoted in LXX form. The concentration in Deut 6-8 is not incidental: these are the chapters on Israel's wilderness fidelity, so Jesus literally answers with the script Israel failed to keep. (Matthew and Luke order the second and third temptations differently; the Deut sources are identical.)
scholarship: France, NIGTC Matthew, on the Deut citations
Kloppenborg, Excavating Q (on the Q temptation as a scribal composition)

references.speaker: Satan
references.note: The tempter cites Scripture: Psalm 91:11-12 ('he will command his angels concerning you... lest you strike your foot against a stone'), LXX. A speaker other than Jesus -- the antagonist -- quoting an apparently apt proof-text, met by counter-citation. ZEITGEIST IRONY: Psalm 91 was the protective/apotropaic psalm par excellence, paired with anti-demonic incantations in the Qumran exorcism collection 11Q11 (11QApocryphal Psalms). So the demonic tempter weaponizing the very psalm used to ward off demons is a pointed inversion available to a first-century audience. The exchange also models the canon's own thesis in miniature: citation can be marshalled in either direction, and the speaker matters as much as the text.
scholarship: Kraus, 'Psalm 91 in 11Q11,' and Sanders DJD on 11Q11

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Eden / new-Adam animal-peace (Isa 11:6-8; cf. Adam at peace with beasts); alternative: hostile beasts (Ps 22; T. Naph. 8:4)
references.note: Mark alone adds 'and he was with the wild beasts, and the angels served him.' Two readings, and the choice is interpretive. (i) New-Adam / restored-Eden: peace with the animals as in the messianic-age oracle Isa 11:6-8, Jesus as the second Adam at home among the beasts a paradise regained. (ii) Hostile beasts as a danger he is preserved through (cf. Ps 22:12-21; Test. Naphtali 8:4, where the devil flees and 'wild beasts will fear you'). The Eden reading is rendered probable -- the angelic ministry favors a paradise-restored tableau -- with the alternative flagged, not suppressed.
scholarship: Bauckham, 'Jesus and the Wild Animals,' in Jesus of Nazareth: Lord and Christ

references.speaker: John
references.source: Lamb imagery (contested): Passover lamb (Exod 12); Servant 'as a lamb led to slaughter' (Isa 53:7); the daily Tamid lamb (Exod 29:38-42); apocalyptic conquering lamb (cf. 1 En., Rev)
references.note: John the Baptist's 'Behold, the Lamb of God' is unmistakably an allusion but the referent is genuinely undecided. Candidates all available in first-century Judaism: the Passover lamb (John's passion is dated to the slaughter of the lambs, 19:14, favoring this), the Isaiah 53 Servant-lamb, the Tamid sacrifice, or the apocalyptic warrior-lamb. Given as a candidate set; the Gospel itself activates more than one. Confidence: established that it alludes; probable as to Passover as the lead sense.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Genesis 28:12 (Jacob's ladder at Bethel); with Gen 27:35 behind 1:47
references.note: 'You will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the son of the human being' rewrites Jacob's dream at Bethel (Gen 28:12), where angels ascend and descend on the ladder/stairway at 'the gate of heaven, the house of God.' Jesus replaces Bethel: the son of humanity is now the junction of heaven and earth. The frame is set two verses earlier when Nathanael is called 'an Israelite in whom there is no guile' (1:47) -- a pointed inversion of Jacob, who took the blessing 'with guile' (Gen 27:35). The whole call scene is staged over the Jacob cycle.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: prophetic-call type-scene (1 Kgs 19:19-21, Elijah calls Elisha); 'fishers of people' OT imagery (Jer 16:16; Ezek 29:4-5; Amos 4:2)
references.note: Two layers. (i) The abrupt leave-everything-and-follow call is the prophetic-call type-scene: Elijah throws his mantle over Elisha at the plough, who abandons the oxen to follow (1 Kgs 19:19-21). Mark's 'immediately they left the nets' reproduces the pattern. Established. (ii) 'Fishers of people' is often traced to Jer 16:16 / Ezek 29:4-5 / Amos 4:2 -- but in every one of those texts the fishing is an image of JUDGMENT (people hauled off to destruction). The cross-reference apparatus does not strongly support the link, and the tension is real: Jesus's usage is positive (gathering for the reign). Marked possible, and the judgment-irony flagged rather than smoothed; this may be a fresh coinage, not an echo.
scholarship: France, NIGTC Matthew, on 4:19 (skeptical of the Jeremiah echo)

references.speaker: other
references.source: Isaiah 6:5 (prophetic-call unworthiness response)
references.note: In Luke's miraculous-catch version, Peter's reaction to the sign -- 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man' -- echoes the prophet's self-abasement at commissioning, paradigmatically Isaiah's 'Woe is me... I am a man of unclean lips' (Isa 6:5). The catch functions as an epiphany that triggers the call. Probable.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: eschatological wine-abundance: Amos 9:13-14; Joel 3:18 [MT 4:18]; Isaiah 25:6; Jeremiah 31:12
references.note: The sheer quantity -- six stone jars, perhaps 120-180 gallons of the best wine -- signals the messianic age, which the prophets imaged as mountains dripping new wine and a banquet of well-aged wines (Amos 9:13-14; Joel 3:18; Isa 25:6 the feast 'of wine on the lees'; Jer 31:12). The sign is read against this Jewish eschatological-abundance stream. Probable-to-established as background.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Dionysus wine-miracle epiphany (Pausanias 6.26.1-2, the Elis kettles; Pliny NH 2.231 and 31.16, the Andros wine-spring)
references.note: THE first history-of-religions flashpoint in the canon. Dionysus, god of wine, was credited with wine-miracles: at Elis three sealed empty kettles filled with wine overnight; on Andros a spring ran with wine at the festival -- both falling near early January, the season later assigned to Cana's commemoration. The wine-god miracle was unquestionably in the Hellenistic air. BUT direction of dependence is sharply contested. Bultmann and the older history-of-religions school read Cana as Christianized Dionysus; many since stress the differences -- no possession, no frenzy, no epiphany of the god's power as such; Jesus is reluctant ('my hour has not yet come'), the wine serves a human wedding, and the meaning is drawn from Jewish messianic abundance (II.2-a), not Greek ecstasy. Held as POSSIBLE ambient resonance, NOT a source (direction: available-convention, not cites). DIVERGENCE: where the Dionysian miracle manifests the god, John's sign is restrained and points away from itself to 'glory' and faith. Flagged, not asserted -- this is precisely the kind of parallel the apparatus exists to weigh in the open.
scholarship: Bultmann, The Gospel of John, 118-120 (the Dionysian proposal)
Hengel, 'The Interpretation of the Wine Miracle at Cana,' in The Glory of Christ in the NT
Keener, Gospel of John, 1:497-500 (the case against direct dependence)
on the parallelomania hazard: Smith, Drudgery Divine

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Jewish purification practice; water-of-purification -> wine-of-the-new-age replacement motif
references.note: John specifies the jars were 'for the Jewish rites of purification.' The transformation of purification-water into celebratory wine is a deliberate replacement motif characteristic of John (cf. the temple, the well, the festivals -- Jesus supersedes the institution). Historical-cultural and motival; probable.

II.3.placement_flag: DISPUTED: John places the cleansing at the start; the Synoptics at the final week. Synoptic cleansing and its citations (Isa 56:7 + Jer 7:11) are handled at Part X. This entry covers John's distinct citation-base only.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Psalm 69:9 [LXX 68:10]
references.note: The disciples recall 'Zeal for your house will consume me' = Psalm 69:9 LXX. John shifts the verb to the future ('will consume') where the Hebrew/LXX reads past ('has consumed'), bending the citation toward the passion -- zeal for the house is what will get Jesus killed. Psalm 69 is one of the principal passion psalms, mined again at the crucifixion (the vinegar, 19:28-29). Established.
scholarship: Menken, Old Testament Quotations in the Fourth Gospel, ch. on Ps 69

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Zechariah 14:21 ('no longer a trader in the house of YHWH of hosts')
references.note: John's Jesus says 'do not make my Father's house a house of trade (emporion)' -- distinct from the Synoptic 'den of robbers.' The wording alludes to Zechariah 14:21, the eschatological vision in which 'there shall no longer be a trader (Canaanite/merchant) in the house of YHWH of hosts on that day.' John's cleansing is keyed to Zechariah's day-of-the-LORD, not to the Isaiah/Jeremiah pair the Synoptics use. Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: eschatological new-temple expectation (Ezek 40-48; 11QTemple; Tob 14:5); temple-as-body
references.note: 'Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it' trades on the live Second Temple hope for a renewed/eschatological temple (Ezekiel's visionary temple; the Temple Scroll; Tobit 14:5), which John redirects to Jesus's body. The same saying surfaces, garbled, at the Synoptic trial (Mark 14:58; 15:29) -- cross-reference to Part X. Probable; the body-temple reading is the narrator's own gloss (2:21).
scholarship: Marcus, AYB Mark, on 14:58 (the temple-saying tradition)

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Ezekiel 36:25-27 (clean water + new spirit); pneuma/wind wordplay at 3:8
references.note: 'Born of water and spirit' pairs the two terms of Ezekiel's new-covenant promise: 'I will sprinkle clean water on you... and a new spirit I will put within you' (Ezek 36:25-27). At 3:8 the discourse exploits pneuma = wind/breath/spirit: 'the wind/spirit blows where it wills.' The double sense is untranslatable and should be preserved (glossary: pneuma). Probable for the Ezekiel background.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Numbers 21:8-9 (the bronze serpent); reception in Wisdom 16:5-7; cf. 2 Kgs 18:4
references.note: 'As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the son of humanity be lifted up' cites Numbers 21:8-9: those bitten who looked at the bronze serpent on the pole lived. The 'lifting up' (hypsoO) puns on crucifixion-and-exaltation. ZEITGEIST: the episode was already being reinterpreted -- Wisdom of Solomon 16:5-7 insists the serpent was 'a symbol of salvation' and that people were saved not by what they saw but by God the savior of all; and 2 Kings 18:4 records Hezekiah destroying the same bronze serpent (Nehushtan) once it became an idol. So John reaches for an OT image whose meaning was already contested and moralized. Established.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Genesis 22:2,16 (the Aqedah: 'your only son, whom you love')
references.note: 'God so loved the world that he gave his only son' may echo the Aqedah, where God commends Abraham 'because you have not withheld your only son' (Gen 22:16; cf. 22:2 'your son, your only son, whom you love'). The giving-up-of-the-only-son resonance is suggestive and joins the agapEtos thread at the baptism (I.2-b), but is not marked as citation. Possible; contested.
scholarship: Levenson, The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son

references.speaker: John
references.source: covenant marriage metaphor (Hos 2; Isa 62:5; Jer 2:2); the 'friend of the bridegroom' (shoshbin) wedding role
references.note: John casts himself as 'the friend of the bridegroom' who rejoices at the bridegroom's voice. The bridegroom is a covenant image: YHWH weds Israel (Hosea 2; Isa 62:5; Jer 2:2), here transferred to Jesus -- joining the bridegroom motif that runs through the Samaritan-woman scene (II.6) and the fasting question (Mark 2:19). The 'friend of the bridegroom' is the Jewish wedding attendant (shoshbin). This discourse is mostly theological reflection and otherwise light on citation. Probable.

II.6.canon_title: The Samaritan woman at the well

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: OT betrothal-at-the-well type-scene: Gen 24 (Rebekah); Gen 29:1-12 (Rachel); Exod 2:15-22 (Zipporah)
references.note: The premier type-scene in the canon. The Torah has a fixed template: a man travels to a foreign land, meets a woman at a well, water is drawn, the woman runs home, a betrothal follows (Isaac/Rebekah, Jacob/Rachel, Moses/Zipporah). John switches it on -- a stranger at Jacob's own well, a woman, the drawing of water, her run to the town -- and SUBVERTS it: there is no betrothal; she has had five husbands and the present man is not her husband; the 'living water' supplants the well; the bridegroom (II.5) is present in a wholly transposed key. The audience that knew the template would feel the swerve, and the swerve is the meaning. Established (a recognized evocation since Alter's analysis).
scholarship: Alter, The Art of Biblical Narrative, ch. 3 ('the type-scene')

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: living water: Jeremiah 2:13; 17:13; Zechariah 14:8; Isaiah 12:3; 55:1; 49:10
references.note: 'Living water' is literally flowing/spring water, but the discourse activates the OT metaphor in which YHWH himself is 'the fountain of living water' whom Israel forsook (Jer 2:13; 17:13), with the eschatological living-waters flowing from Jerusalem (Zech 14:8) and the wells of salvation (Isa 12:3; 55:1). Since in Jeremiah the fountain IS God, Jesus offering living water is a pointed self-implication. The double sense (spring-water / Spirit) is the hinge of the dialogue and should be preserved. Established background.
scholarship: Menken, OT Quotations in the Fourth Gospel

references.speaker: other
references.source: Samaritan-Jewish cult dispute; Mount Gerizim (Deut 27:12; Samaritan Pentateuch)
references.note: 'Our fathers worshiped on this mountain' refers to the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim (sanctioned in the Samaritan Pentateuch's reading of Deut 27 and the Decalogue), destroyed by John Hyrcanus c. 128 BCE -- a wound still raw in the first century. Historical-cultural background the modern reader cannot supply unaided. Established.

references.speaker: other
references.source: Samaritan messianic expectation (the Taheb), rooted in the prophet-like-Moses of Deuteronomy 18:15-18
references.note: The woman's 'I know that Messiah is coming' reflects distinctively Samaritan eschatology: rejecting the prophets and Davidic kingship, Samaritans awaited the Taheb ('the Restorer'), a Mosaic prophet on the model of Deut 18:15-18. The precise first-century form of Taheb belief is debated, so probable rather than established, but the Mosaic-prophet expectation is secure and explains why John frames the disclosure here as prophet-recognition.

II.7.canon_title: Return to Galilee; the official's son

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: inner-canon parallel: the centurion's servant (Matt 8:5-13 // Luke 7:1-10) -- handled at Part V
references.note: The healing-at-a-distance of a Capernaum official's son is widely held to be a Johannine form of the centurion's-servant tradition (Matt 8 // Luke 7): same town, same long-distance cure, same faith-of-the-petitioner emphasis. Whether they are one tradition or two similar episodes is contested. Logged as an inner-canon cross-reference (to Part V), not an external allusion. Possible.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: the prophet-without-honor logion: Mark 6:4 // Matt 13:57 // Luke 4:24 // Thomas 31 // P.Oxy 1.30-35
references.note: 'A prophet has no honor in his own country' is one of the most strongly multiply-attested sayings of Jesus -- in Mark, Matthew, Luke, John, AND Thomas/P.Oxy 1 independently. Multiple attestation across independent streams is a leading criterion of authenticity. Cross-reference to the Nazareth rejection (II.9-c), where Luke pairs it with the physician proverb exactly as Thomas 31 does. Established.
scholarship: Meier, A Marginal Jew, on multiple attestation
DeConick, The Original Gospel of Thomas, on logion 31

references.speaker: narrator
references.note: Matthew's formula citation: 'Galilee of the nations -- the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light' = Isaiah 9:1-2, in Matthew's characteristic abridged, non-LXX form. The point is geographic-theological: the messianic light dawns in despised, half-Gentile Galilee. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: kingdom-of-God announcement; herald of good news (Isa 52:7); the everlasting kingdom (Dan 2:44; 7:14)
references.note: 'The reign of God has drawn near; turn (metanoeite) and trust the good news' is the programmatic announcement. Its vocabulary draws on Isaiah 52:7 -- the herald who 'brings good news (euangelizomai)... saying to Zion, your God reigns' -- and the Daniel hope of an everlasting kingdom (2:44; 7:14). basileia, metanoia, and euangelion are all glossary terms; the imminence ('has drawn near') is the disputed eschatological crux. Probable for the Isa 52:7 herald background; established as kingdom-announcement language.
scholarship: Beasley-Murray, Jesus and the Kingdom of God

II.9.placement_flag: DISPUTED / possible duplicate with Mark 6:1-6 // Matt 13:53-58 (Part VII).

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Isaiah 61:1-2a, spliced with Isaiah 58:6; deliberately stopping before 61:2b
references.note: The programmatic citation of the canon. Jesus reads Isaiah 61:1-2 (the Spirit-anointed herald: good news to the poor, release to captives, sight to the blind, the year of the LORD's favor), splices in 'to set the oppressed free' from Isaiah 58:6, and -- crucially -- STOPS mid-verse, omitting 61:2b 'and the day of vengeance of our God.' The editorial cut IS the message: Jesus defines his mission as favor and release without the vengeance-on-the-nations his hearers awaited. This is the strongest case in the canon so far of the omission carrying the meaning -- what is NOT quoted is as decisive as what is. ZEITGEIST: Isaiah 61's jubilee-release was already read messianically at Qumran, where 11QMelchizedek (11Q13) assigns its 'liberty' and 'year of favor' to an eschatological deliverer -- so Jesus claims a text already charged with end-time liberation, and then pointedly truncates it. Established.
scholarship: Sanders, 'From Isaiah 61 to Luke 4,' in Luke and Scripture

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: proverb 'Physician, heal yourself' (widely attested Greco-Roman and Jewish; cf. Gen. Rab. 23:4)
references.note: 'Physician, heal yourself' is a floating proverb attested across Greek and Jewish sources; Jesus quotes it as the taunt he anticipates. Notably Thomas 31 pairs the physician saying with the prophet saying -- the same pairing Luke makes here (4:23-24). Probable as a proverb in the zeitgeist.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on logion 31

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: prophet-without-honor logion (Mark 6:4 // Matt 13:57 // John 4:44 // Thomas 31 // P.Oxy 1.30-35)
references.note: 'No prophet is acceptable in his own country.' Cross-reference to II.7-b. The remarkable datum: Thomas 31 ('no prophet is accepted in his own village; no physician heals those who know him') yokes the prophet and physician sayings together exactly as Luke does at 4:23-24, an agreement between Luke and Thomas that bears on their tradition-relationship. Established by multiple attestation.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on logion 31
Plisch, The Gospel of Thomas, on 31

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: 1 Kings 17:8-24 (Elijah and the widow of Zarephath); 2 Kings 5:1-14 (Elisha and Naaman the Syrian)
references.note: Jesus cites two prophetic precedents -- Elijah sent not to Israel's widows but to a Sidonian widow (1 Kgs 17), Elisha cleansing not Israel's lepers but the Syrian Naaman (2 Kgs 5) -- as scriptural warrant that God's favor runs past Israel to outsiders. This is Jesus deploying narrative Scripture as argument, and it is the provocation that turns the synagogue murderous (4:28-29). A clear speaker-cites-Scripture entry, and a programmatic statement of the boundary-crossing mission. Established.
scholarship: Brodie, 'Towards Unravelling Luke's Use of the Old Testament: Luke 7:11-17 and 1 Kings 17'

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: ancient exorcism contest: Josephus, Ant. 8.46-49 (Eleazar); the magical papyri (PGM); Qumran exorcism texts (11Q11; 4Q560; Genesis Apocryphon 1QapGen 20)
references.note: The scene runs on the conventions of ancient exorcism, which the first-century audience knew as a recognizable contest. The demon's opening move -- 'I know who you are, the Holy One of God' -- is the standard defensive gambit: to name a spirit precisely is to bid for mastery over it (cf. the adjuration-by-name formulae throughout the magical papyri and the Qumran incantations). DIVERGENCE, and it is the whole point: Jesus answers with none of the apparatus the convention requires -- no incantation, no invocation of a higher name, no ring or root (contrast Eleazar's ring in Josephus) -- only a bare command, 'Be muzzled, and come out.' The crowd's astonishment is at the unmediated authority. Established.

references.speaker: other
references.source: 'the Holy One of God': Psalm 106:16 (Aaron, 'the holy one of YHWH'); Judges 13:7; 16:17 LXX (Samson)
references.note: The demon's title 'the Holy One of God' is rare; the nearest scriptural anchors are Aaron, 'the holy one of YHWH' (Ps 106:16), and the nazirite Samson, 'holy one of God' (Judg 16:17 LXX). The echo is faint and the title may simply mark Jesus as the one set apart by/for God. Possible.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Isaiah 53:4
references.note: Matthew caps the healing summary with Isaiah 53:4: 'He took our infirmities and bore our diseases.' TEXT-FORM showcase: Matthew renders the line for PHYSICAL illness, tracking the Hebrew, and pointedly NOT the LXX, which spiritualizes Isa 53:4 ('he bears our sins'). The evangelist bypasses the Greek Bible because only the literal-illness sense fits a healing report -- the text-form is chosen by the application. This binds the suffering Servant (Isa 53) to the healing ministry, alongside Isa 42 at the baptism (I.2-b) and at III.10.
scholarship: Menken, Matthew's Bible, ch. on Isa 53:4

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: prophetic withdrawal to a deserted place to pray (cf. Elijah, 1 Kgs 19:3-12)
references.note: Jesus withdraws before dawn to a deserted place (erEmos topos) to pray -- a recurrent Markan habit that draws lightly on the prophetic-solitude topos (Elijah to Horeb). This pericope is otherwise thin intertextually; logged at possible so the section's coverage stays honest rather than padded.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Leviticus 14:1-32 (priestly purification of the healed leper); background Leviticus 13-14
references.note: 'Show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded' directs the man to the rite of Leviticus 14:1-32. Jesus cites Torah law and upholds it -- the cleansing is referred back into the priestly purity system (Lev 13-14), whose social-religious exclusion of the leper is the background the modern reader needs to feel the stakes. Established.
scholarship: Milgrom, Leviticus 1-16 (AYB), on the metsora rite

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: 2 Kings 5:1-14 (Elisha cleanses Naaman's leprosy)
references.note: As the principal OT leprosy-cleansing narrative -- and the very text Jesus invoked at Nazareth (II.9-d) -- 2 Kings 5 stands behind the episode, casting Jesus in the Elisha role of the prophet who cleanses. Possible; the resonance is thematic, not verbal. NOTE: Mark 1:41's 'moved with compassion' vs. the Western variant 'moved with anger' (orgistheis) is a pure text-critical crux and belongs to the text-critical layer, not this apparatus.

III.5.canon_title: The paralytic let down through the roof

references.speaker: other
references.source: the divine prerogative of pardon: Isaiah 43:25; Exodus 34:6-7; Micah 7:18; Daniel 9:9
references.note: The scribes' objection -- 'who can forgive sins but God alone?' -- invokes a settled scriptural axiom: it is YHWH who blots out transgressions (Isa 43:25, 'I, I am he'), who forgives iniquity (Exod 34:6-7; Mic 7:18; Dan 9:9). The objection is theologically correct on its own terms, which is what makes the pronouncement provocative. Speaker is the objectors. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Daniel 7:13-14 (the one like a son of man given authority and dominion)
references.note: 'The son of the human being has authority on earth to forgive sins' first sounds the authority-claim that the Danielic son-of-man carries (Dan 7:13-14, given dominion). Whether 'son of the human being' here is titular (Danielic) or the Aramaic bar enasha idiom ('a human being / one in my position') is the standing crux flagged under the divine-names policy (huios tou anthrOpou rendered 'the son of the human being'; Daniel 7 footnoted at first occurrence). The authority-to-forgive, exercised on earth, leans Danielic. Probable.
scholarship: Marcus, AYB Mark, on 2:10 and 'Son of Man'
Casey, The Solution to the Son of Man Problem (the bar enasha case)

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Psalm 103:3 (forgives iniquity / heals diseases); cf. Psalm 41:4
references.note: The story's logic -- the visible cure validating the invisible pardon -- rests on the ancient pairing of forgiveness and healing, classically Psalm 103:3, 'who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases' (cf. Ps 41:4, where sin and sickness are linked). The healing is offered as the demonstrable sign of the harder, unseen forgiveness. Probable.

III.6.canon_title: Call of Levi; eating with sinners

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Hosea 6:6 ('I desire mercy, not sacrifice')
references.note: Matthew alone inserts Hosea 6:6 -- 'go and learn what this means: I desire mercy (eleos / Heb. hesed), not sacrifice' -- which Mark and Luke lack, and which Matthew deploys a second time at 12:7. A redactional addition that recruits the prophetic critique of cult to defend table-fellowship with sinners. Speaker Jesus (in Matthew's form). Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the physician proverb (cf. II.9-b, Luke 4:23; widely attested Greco-Roman)
references.note: 'Those who are strong have no need of a physician, but those who are sick' is the floating physician proverb, met already at Nazareth (II.9-b). Jesus turns the commonplace into a defense of his mission to the 'sick.' Probable as ambient proverb.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: non-canonical parallel: P.Oxy 1224
references.note: The fragmentary P.Oxy 1224 preserves an independent form of this meal-controversy. Its distinctive feature is an expanded list of objectors -- 'the scribes and Pharisees and priests' -- adding the priests, before the physician saying follows. The papyrus is damaged and the reconstruction partial, so the witness is treated cautiously, but it attests the scene outside the Synoptic stream. Probable.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: table-fellowship as social-religious boundary; toll-collectors and 'sinners' (hamartOloi)
references.note: Sharing a table signified acceptance and incurred shared purity status, which is why eating with toll-collectors (collaborator-impure, handling Gentile coin) and 'sinners' (those living outside Torah observance) was a public scandal, not mere bad company. The historical-cultural background the modern reader needs to register the offense. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: covenant-bridegroom imagery (Hos 2; Isa 62:5); cf. II.5-a
references.note: 'Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them?' draws on the covenant-bridegroom image (YHWH wedding Israel, Hos 2; Isa 62:5), threaded through the canon at II.5-a and II.6. 'The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them' (2:20) is Mark's first veiled passion-hint, smuggled inside a wedding metaphor. Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallel: Gospel of Thomas 47 (patch + wineskins + old/new wine)
references.note: The twin similitudes -- unshrunk patch on an old garment, new wine in old skins -- are independently attested at Thomas 47, which also carries the extra line 'no one drinks old wine and immediately wants new,' a sapiential coda the Synoptics lack (Luke 5:39 preserves a related remark). The proverbial-wisdom form (paired similitudes) is the vehicle; the parallel is established.
scholarship: DeConick, The Original Gospel of Thomas, on logion 47
Plisch, The Gospel of Thomas, on 47

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: 1 Samuel 21:1-6 (David eats the bread of the Presence); Leviticus 24:5-9 (the showbread reserved to priests)
references.note: Jesus cites David's eating of the bread of the Presence at Nob (1 Sam 21:1-6), bread lawful only for priests (Lev 24:5-9), as the precedent that human need overrides cultic restriction. Speaker Jesus; a scriptural argument from precedent. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: citation error: Mark names Abiathar; 1 Samuel 21 names AHIMELECH (Abiathar's father)
references.note: SHOWCASE of the apparatus's recurring pattern. Mark sets the episode 'in the days of Abiathar the high priest,' but 1 Samuel 21 names Ahimelech, Abiathar's father; Abiathar succeeds him only later. Mark's slip. And exactly as with the 'Isaiah' mis-attribution (I.1-a), BOTH Matthew (12:3-4) and Luke (6:3-4) independently DELETE the Abiathar clause -- two later evangelists silently repairing a Markan citation-error. The cleanup is itself evidence: it points to Markan priority and confirms the canon-wide tendency of the later tradition to tidy the earlier. Established.
scholarship: Marcus, AYB Mark, on 2:26 (the Abiathar problem)

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: rabbinic maxim: Mekhilta on Exod 31:14 (R. Shimon b. Menasya, 'the Sabbath is given to you, not you to the Sabbath')
references.note: 'The Sabbath was made for the human being, not the human being for the Sabbath' is closely paralleled by the later rabbinic maxim in the Mekhilta (R. Shimon b. Menasya). DIRECTION/DATING DISCIPLINE: the Mekhilta postdates Mark by centuries, so this is NOT Mark citing the rabbis nor the reverse -- the principle was evidently a shared, probably proverbial, Sabbath-axiom in circulation. Flagged as shared-tradition, not dependence. Probable.
scholarship: Marcus, AYB Mark, on 2:27 (with the dating caveat)

III.9.canon_title: The man with the withered hand

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Second Temple Sabbath/life-saving debate: 1 Macc 2:29-41; CD 11:13-17 (Qumran stringency); m. Yoma 8:6 (pikuach nefesh)
references.note: 'Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?' plants Jesus inside a real, contested first-century halakhic debate. The Maccabean crisis forced a ruling that one may fight to save life on the Sabbath (1 Macc 2:29-41); Qumran took the stringent line (CD 11:13-17 forbids even hauling an animal from a pit on the Sabbath); the Pharisaic-rabbinic tradition permitted overriding the Sabbath to save life (pikuach nefesh, later codified at m. Yoma 8:6). Jesus stakes out the life-prioritizing pole of a live argument, not a timeless abstraction. Established.
scholarship: Doering, Schabbat (on Second Temple Sabbath halakhah)

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: the hardened-heart motif (Isa 6:10; Ps 95:8; Exod 4-14); kardia
references.note: Jesus is 'grieved at the hardness of their heart' (pOrOsis tEs kardias) -- the hardened-heart motif of the prophets and the Exodus (Isa 6:10; Ps 95:8; the hardening of Pharaoh). kardia carries the Hebraic sense of the seat of will, not feeling (glossary). Possible-to-probable as motif.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Isaiah 42:1-4 (the first Servant Song)
references.note: Matthew's longest formula citation: Isaiah 42:1-4, applied to Jesus's withdrawal and his order of silence. 'He will not wrangle or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets; a bruised reed he will not break' reads the so-called messianic secret as the quiet, non-clamorous Servant fulfilling prophecy; the closing 'in his name the nations will hope' follows the LXX and opens the Gentile horizon. TEXT-FORM: a composite rendering, neither pure LXX nor MT. Binds Isa 42 (already heard at the baptism, I.2-b) to the healing ministry. Established.
scholarship: Menken, Matthew's Bible, ch. on Isa 42

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: the Twelve as the twelve tribes (eschatological restoration of Israel); cf. Matt 19:28 // Luke 22:30; 1QS 8:1
references.note: Appointing exactly twelve is a symbolic claim: it reconstitutes the twelve tribes, casting Jesus's movement as restored Israel. The symbolism is made explicit later -- the Twelve will 'judge the twelve tribes of Israel' (Matt 19:28 // Luke 22:30) -- and the number-based council has an analogue at Qumran (1QS 8:1, a council with a twelve-fold core). The figure is an eschatological statement, not an administrative one. Established.
scholarship: Sanders, Jesus and Judaism, on the Twelve and the restoration of Israel

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: mountain as locus of appointment/revelation (Sinai); the renaming-marks-vocation motif (Gen 17:5; 32:28)
references.note: 'He went up the mountain' stages the appointment on the mountain of revelation (Moses-Sinai overtones), and the renaming -- Simon to Peter, the sons of Zebedee to Boanerges -- follows the biblical pattern in which a new name marks a new vocation (Abram to Abraham, Gen 17:5; Jacob to Israel, Gen 32:28). Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Isaiah 61:1-2 (good news to the poor; comfort for mourners); Psalm 37:11 (the meek inherit the land)
references.note: The opening beatitudes unpack Isaiah 61:1-2 -- the very manifesto Jesus claimed and truncated at Nazareth (II.9-a): good news to the POOR, comfort to those who MOURN. 'The meek shall inherit the earth' (5:5) is Psalm 37:11 nearly verbatim (LXX 36:11). So the Sermon opens by spelling out the Isaiah-61 program in beatitude form. Established; direct line to II.9-a.
scholarship: Betz, Hermeneia: The Sermon on the Mount, on 5:3-12
Davies-Allison, ICC Matthew I, on the Beatitudes

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the macarism (beatitude) form: Ps 1:1; Sir 25:7-10; 4QBeatitudes (4Q525); the prophetic reversal (1 Sam 2:1-10; Isa 29:19)
references.note: The blessing-formula ('blessed/happy is the one who...') is a standing biblical and sapiential genre (Ps 1; Sirach), and a beatitude-SERIES like Jesus's is paralleled at Qumran in 4Q525 -- the form was alive and serialized in the zeitgeist. Luke's matching woes (6:24-26) make explicit the prophetic great-reversal pattern (Hannah's song, the Magnificat): the lowly lifted, the comfortable cast down. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallel: Gospel of Thomas 54
references.note: Thomas 54 ('Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of heaven') is a useful witness to the saying's earliest shape: it reads 'the poor' (with Luke, against Matthew's spiritualizing 'poor in spirit') yet 'kingdom of heaven' (with Matthew, against Luke's 'kingdom of God'). A split agreement bearing on the tradition-history of the first beatitude. Established.
scholarship: DeConick, The Original Gospel of Thomas, on logion 54
Plisch, The Gospel of Thomas, on 54

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: salt of the covenant (Lev 2:13; Num 18:19); light to the nations (Isa 42:6; 49:6; 60:1-3); city-on-a-hill (Thomas 32)
references.note: Two covenant images. Salt carries the 'covenant of salt' freight (Lev 2:13; Num 18:19), here turned to discipleship's preservative role; light draws on Israel/Servant as 'light to the nations' (Isa 42:6; 49:6; 60:1-3). The 'city set on a hill' is independently attested at Thomas 32 ('a city built on a high mountain and fortified cannot fall'), and the lamp-on-a-stand at Thomas 33 (cf. Mark 4:21, handled at VI). Probable.
scholarship: Betz, Hermeneia: Sermon on the Mount, on 5:13-16
DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 32-33

IV.3.canon_title: Law and the prophets; the antitheses

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the permanence of Torah (cf. Luke 16:17; Bar 4:1); the iota/keraia = the yod and the scribal stroke
references.note: The programmatic frame for the antitheses: not to abolish but to fulfill the law and the prophets; 'not one iota (the smallest letter, yod) or stroke (keraia) will pass.' Luke preserves the same maxim independently (16:17). The affirmation of Torah's enduring validity is the backdrop against which the 'but I say to you' formulas must be read -- intensification, not abrogation. Established.
scholarship: Betz, Hermeneia: Sermon on the Mount, on 5:17-20

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Exodus 20:13 // Deuteronomy 5:17 ('you shall not kill')
references.note: Antithesis 1. Cites the Decalogue's prohibition of murder and drives it back to its root in anger and contempt ('raca,' an Aramaic insult; the threat of Gehenna -- the Valley of Hinnom, Jerusalem's refuse-fire, as image of judgment). The citation is upheld and radicalized to the disposition behind the act. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Exodus 20:14 // Deuteronomy 5:18 ('you shall not commit adultery')
references.note: Antithesis 2. Cites the Decalogue on adultery and relocates the offense to the lustful look -- the act traced to the intention. The hyperbolic 'tear out the eye' belongs to the same interiorizing move. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Leviticus 19:12; Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:21-23 (oaths and vows); cf. the Essene avoidance of oaths (Josephus, War 2.135); Jas 5:12
references.note: Antithesis 4 (oaths). Composite citation of the oath/vow legislation (Lev 19:12, do not swear falsely by the name; Num 30:2; Deut 23:21). Jesus abolishes oath-taking entirely ('let your yes be yes'), a stringency paralleled among the Essenes, who Josephus says shunned oaths as worse than perjury (War 2.135), and echoed at James 5:12. ZEITGEIST: oath-avoidance was a recognizable piety, not a novelty. Established.
scholarship: Betz, Hermeneia: Sermon on the Mount, on 5:33-37
Davies-Allison, ICC Matthew I, ad loc.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the lex talionis: Exodus 21:24; Leviticus 24:19-20; Deuteronomy 19:21 ('eye for eye')
references.note: Antithesis 5. Cites the talion law (Exod 21:24; Lev 24:20; Deut 19:21). The crucial background: the talion was itself a LIMIT on vengeance -- proportional, capping retaliation at the equivalent. Jesus extends the trajectory past proportionality to non-retaliation (turn the cheek, give the cloak, go the second mile). The counter-ruling completes a vector the Torah had already started. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Leviticus 19:18 ('love your neighbor'); 'hate your enemy' = NOT Torah -- nearest: Qumran 1QS 1:3-4,9-10; cf. Ps 139:21-22
references.note: Antithesis 6, and the most revealing. 'Love your neighbor' is Leviticus 19:18; but 'and hate your enemy' is NOWHERE in the Torah. The nearest formal source is the Qumran Community Rule, which commands loving 'the sons of light' and hating 'the sons of darkness' (1QS 1:3-4, 9-10); cf. the psalmist's 'I hate them with perfect hatred' (Ps 139:21-22). So the 'you have heard' may quote a real sectarian halakhah in the air, not Scripture -- and Jesus counters it with enemy-love grounded in the impartial Father who sends sun and rain on all. CONFIDENCE: established for Lev 19:18; probable that 1QS-type teaching is the target of 'hate your enemy.'

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Deuteronomy 24:1 (the certificate of divorce) countered by Genesis 1:27 + 2:24 (creation: one flesh); cf. CD 4:20-5:2; the Hillel/Shammai debate (m. Gittin 9:10)
references.note: Jesus sets Scripture against Scripture: the Mosaic concession of a divorce-certificate (Deut 24:1) is subordinated to the creation order, Genesis 1:27 ('male and female') and 2:24 ('the two become one flesh'), read as the prior and binding will. ZEITGEIST: the Damascus Document deploys the SAME Genesis 1:27 prooftext ('male and female he created them') against divorce and polygamy (CD 4:20-5:2) -- so Jesus's creation-over-concession argument has a direct Qumran analogue. The whole exchange sits inside the live Hillel/Shammai divorce debate (m. Gittin 9:10: any cause vs. unchastity only), with Jesus stricter than both. Established.
scholarship: Instone-Brewer, Divorce and Remarriage in the Bible

references.speaker: other
references.source: inner-canon: Paul citing a dominical command ('not I, but the Lord')
references.note: Paul, writing in the mid-50s -- earlier than any Gospel -- expressly cites Jesus's divorce ruling: 'to the married I give charge, not I but the LORD, that a wife should not separate from her husband.' This is the earliest datable attestation of the teaching and a model of the canon's inclusion logic: Paul here functions as a REPORTER of dominical tradition ('not I but the Lord'), explicitly distinguishing the Lord's command from his own counsel two verses later (7:12, 'I say, not the Lord'). Established; valuable as pre-Gospel witness.
scholarship: Hengel and Schwemer, on early dominical tradition

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the three pillars of Jewish piety -- almsgiving, prayer, fasting (Tobit 12:8); hypokritEs = the stage-actor
references.note: The section is structured on the three classic acts of Jewish righteousness -- almsgiving (tsedaqah), prayer, and fasting -- already triadically linked in Tobit 12:8. Jesus does not abolish them; he targets their performance for an audience. The repeated 'hypocrites' is theatrical vocabulary -- hypokritEs is the masked stage-actor -- framing public piety as playing to a crowd for the wage of being seen. Established.
scholarship: Betz, Hermeneia: Sermon on the Mount, on 6:1-18

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the Kaddish (sanctify the great name; establish the kingdom); Ezekiel 36:23; cf. the Amidah
references.note: The opening petitions track the synagogue Kaddish almost step for step -- 'may his great name be magnified and SANCTIFIED... may he establish his KINGDOM' answers 'hallowed be your name, your kingdom come.' 'Hallowed be your name' rests on Ezekiel 36:23, 'I will sanctify my great name,' and the petitions sit within the Eighteen Benedictions (Amidah) tradition. The prayer is a distilled Jewish liturgy, not a departure from one. Established.
scholarship: Betz, Hermeneia: Sermon on the Mount, on the Lord's Prayer
on the Kaddish parallel: Jeremias, The Prayers of Jesus

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: debt-release / Jubilee: Deuteronomy 15:1-2 (shemittah); Leviticus 25 (Jubilee); the aphesis word-group
references.note: 'Forgive us our debts (opheilEmata) as we forgive our debtors' uses the debt-idiom for sin (Aramaic hoba = debt/sin) and trades on the sabbatical/Jubilee release of debts (Deut 15:1-2; Lev 25), the same aphesis ('release') word Jesus read from Isaiah 61 at Nazareth (II.9-a). Sin as debt, forgiveness as release -- the economic metaphor is load-bearing and should not be flattened to 'trespasses.' Probable.
scholarship: Anderson, Sin: A History (on the debt-metaphor)

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: non-canonical reception: Didache 8:2 (the liturgical form + doxology)
references.note: The Didache (c. 100) gives the prayer in close-to-Matthean form WITH the doxology 'for yours is the power and the glory forever,' and directs praying it three times daily -- the earliest evidence of its fixed liturgical use. TEXT-CRITICAL datapoint: the doxology ('for thine is the kingdom, the power, and the glory') is absent from the oldest Matthean manuscripts and present in the Didache, indicating it entered the text from liturgical practice. Established.
scholarship: Metzger, Textual Commentary, on Matt 6:13 (the doxology)

IV.7.canon_title: Treasure in heaven; serving two masters; anxiety

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: treasure in heaven: Tobit 4:8-9; Sirach 29:10-12; 4 Ezra 7:77; cf. Thomas 76
references.note: Storing 'treasure in heaven' is a settled Second Temple idea -- almsgiving and righteous deeds as capital deposited with God (Tobit 4:8-9; Sirach 29:10-12, 'lay up your treasure according to the commandments'; 4 Ezra 7:77). Thomas 76 carries the same image ('where no moth comes near to devour'). The metaphor is conventional; the demand to relocate one's heart there is the point. Established.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 76

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallel: Thomas 47 (no one can serve two masters); mammon = Aramaic mamona (wealth)
references.note: 'No one can serve two masters... you cannot serve God and mammon' is independently attested at Thomas 47, which clusters it with the wineskins and patch sayings (cf. III.7-b). 'Mammon' is the Aramaic mamona, wealth personified as a rival lord. Established.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on logion 47

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallel: P.Oxy 5575 (the worry/anxiety saying)
references.note: The worry-saying ('which of you by being anxious can add a cubit to his span?') is among the sayings preserved on P.Oxy 5575, a recently published papyrus carrying material that overlaps the Sermon and Thomas. FRESHNESS FLAG: the fragment is newly edited and its readings and relationships are still under scholarly assessment, so it is logged at possible rather than established; the witness should be re-checked against the editio princeps as the discussion settles.
scholarship: P.Oxy 5575 (editio princeps, Oxyrhynchus Papyri vol. 87) -- verify readings at build time

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: providential provision: Psalm 147:9 (God feeds the ravens); Job 38:41; cf. 1 Kgs 17 (ravens feed Elijah)
references.note: The birds-and-lilies argument draws on the creation-providence theme: God feeds the ravens (Ps 147:9; Job 38:41) and clothes the wild grass. Luke's form specifies 'ravens' (12:24), sharpening the Psalm 147 allusion. The lesson moves from God's care for the lower creation to the disciple a fortiori. Probable.

IV.8.canon_title: Judging; the speck and the log

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallel: Thomas 26 (speck and log); the measure-for-measure principle (middah k-neged middah; cf. m. Sotah 1:7)
references.note: The speck-and-log saying is independently attested at Thomas 26. The framing maxim, 'with the measure you use it will be measured to you' (7:2), is the rabbinic principle of measure-for-measure (middah k-neged middah; m. Sotah 1:7) -- God's reciprocal justice answering human conduct in kind. Established.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on logion 26

IV.9.canon_title: Ask, seek, knock; the golden rule

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallel: Thomas 92, 94 (seek and find; knock and it opens)
references.note: 'Ask... seek... knock' is multiply attested at Thomas 92 ('seek and you will find') and 94 ('one who seeks will find; to one who knocks it will be opened'). The seek-and-find motif is a Thomasine signature, here shared with Q. Established.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 92, 94

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the golden rule: Leviticus 19:18; negative form in Tobit 4:15 and Hillel (b. Shabbat 31a)
references.note: Jesus's 'do to others whatever you would have them do to you -- this is the law and the prophets' restates Leviticus 19:18 and matches Hillel's summary of the whole Torah (b. Shabbat 31a) and Tobit 4:15. DIVERGENCE worth flagging: the common form in the zeitgeist is NEGATIVE ('what you hate, do to no one' -- Tobit, Hillel); Jesus gives the POSITIVE form ('do...'), which demands initiative rather than mere restraint, while making the same whole-Torah-summary claim. Established.

IV.10.canon_title: The narrow gate; tree and fruit; two foundations

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the Two Ways: Deuteronomy 30:15-19; Jeremiah 21:8; Psalm 1; the Two-Spirits at Qumran (1QS 3:13-4:26); Didache 1-6; Barnabas 18-20
references.note: The two gates / two roads is the Two Ways tradition, a widespread catechetical form: the way of life and the way of death (Deut 30:15-19; Jer 21:8; Ps 1), elaborated at Qumran as the two spirits (1QS 3:13-4:26) and as the structuring frame of the Didache (1-6) and Barnabas (18-20). Jesus invokes a form his hearers already used to map moral choice. Established.
scholarship: Niederwimmer, Hermeneia: The Didache, on the Two Ways

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallel: Thomas 45 (grapes not from thorns; good treasure of the heart)
references.note: 'By their fruits you will know them -- are grapes gathered from thorns?' is independently attested at Thomas 45, which likewise pairs the thorn/fruit image with the good-and-evil treasure of the heart. A sapiential test-by-fruit, shared across Q and Thomas. Established.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 45

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: wisdom-vs-folly building; the storm-tested structure (cf. Ezek 13:10-16; Prov 10:25; 12:7)
references.note: The two builders -- house on rock vs. on sand, tested by flood and wind -- enacts the wisdom/folly contrast of Proverbs (the righteous stand, the wicked are swept off, Prov 10:25; 12:7) and recalls Ezekiel's wall of untempered whitewash that the storm brings down (Ezek 13:10-16). Building and storm as judgment-test. Probable.
scholarship: Betz, Hermeneia: Sermon on the Mount, on 7:24-27
Davies-Allison, ICC Matthew I, ad loc.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: eschatological banquet + Gentile ingathering: Isaiah 25:6-8; Psalm 107:3; Isaiah 49:12; Malachi 1:11
references.note: Provoked by a Gentile's faith, Jesus foretells that 'many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom' while 'the sons of the kingdom' are cast out. This fuses the eschatological feast for all peoples (Isa 25:6-8) with the ingathering from the four directions (Ps 107:3; Isa 49:12; Mal 1:11, the name 'great among the nations'). The reversal -- insiders out, outsiders in -- is the sting. Established.
scholarship: on the eschatological banquet: Isa 25:6-8 with Marcus / Hengel

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: the faith of the Gentile outsider; healing-at-a-distance; cross-ref John 4:46-54 (II.7-a)
references.note: The centurion's trust (pistis) -- praised above any in Israel -- belongs to the recurring motif of the outsider whose faith outstrips the insiders'. The healing-at-a-distance and the Capernaum setting align it with John's official's son (II.7-a); whether these are one tradition or two similar episodes is the open question flagged there. Probable.

V.2.canon_title: Raising the widow's son at Nain

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: 1 Kings 17:17-24 (Elijah raises the widow of Zarephath's son); 2 Kings 4:32-37 (Elisha and the Shunammite's son)
references.note: The most transparent Elijah typology in the canon. Luke raises a WIDOW'S only son and reports 'he gave him to his mother' (7:15) -- verbatim the LXX of 1 Kings 17:23, where Elijah raises the widow of Zarephath's son; the Elisha raising (2 Kgs 4) stands behind it too. The crowd draws the intended inference: 'a great prophet has arisen among us' (7:16). Luke deliberately casts Jesus as Elijah-redivivus -- the same prophet Jesus invoked at Nazareth (II.9-d). Established by the verbal echo.
scholarship: Brodie, 'Towards Unravelling Luke's Use of the OT: Luke 7:11-17 and 1 Kings 17:17-24'

V.3.canon_title: John the Baptist's question; Jesus's reply

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Isaiah catena: 35:5-6; 29:18-19; 42:7; 61:1 -- and Qumran 4Q521 (the Messianic Apocalypse)
references.note: Jesus answers John not with a claim but with a list of works drawn from Isaiah: the blind see and deaf hear (Isa 35:5-6; 29:18), the lame leap (35:6), good news to the poor (61:1). The decisive parallel is the Qumran Messianic Apocalypse, 4Q521, which catalogues the works of God's anointed in almost the same terms -- healing the wounded, GOOD NEWS to the poor, and RAISING THE DEAD. 'Raise the dead' is in neither Isaiah text but stands in BOTH 4Q521 and Jesus's list, showing this exact messianic-works profile was a pre-Christian Jewish expectation already in circulation. A first-rank zeitgeist datapoint. Established.
scholarship: 4Q521 (Messianic Apocalypse); Collins, The Scepter and the Star, on 4Q521

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Malachi 3:1 (+ Exodus 23:20)
references.note: 'Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way' -- the Malachi 3:1 / Exodus 23:20 composite, now on JESUS'S lips about John. CROSS-REF to I.1-a: this is precisely where Matthew and Luke relocated the Malachi half that Mark had wrongly bundled into his 'as written in Isaiah' citation. The pattern closes -- the misplaced messenger-text reappears, correctly, in the mouth of Jesus. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Malachi 4:5-6 [MT 3:23-24] (the returning Elijah)
references.note: 'He is Elijah who is to come' makes explicit the identification staged by John's wardrobe at I.1-c: John is the Elijah of Malachi 4:5-6 who precedes the Day of YHWH. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: personified Wisdom (Sophia): Proverbs 8; Sirach 24; Wisdom of Solomon
references.note: The children-in-the-marketplace parable closes with 'wisdom is justified by her deeds' (Matt) / 'by all her children' (Luke). The figure is personified Wisdom (Prov 8; Sir 24), with John and Jesus as her rejected envoys -- early Wisdom Christology, developed further at V.5. Probable; Luke's 'children' may be the older reading.
scholarship: Suggs, Wisdom, Christology, and Law in Matthew's Gospel

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: judgment-oracle cities (Tyre/Sidon: Isa 23, Ezek 26-28; Sodom: Gen 19, Ezek 16:48-50); 'brought down to Hades' = Isaiah 14:13-15
references.note: The woes invoke the classic prophetic judgment-cities: Tyre and Sidon (Isa 23; Ezek 26-28) and Sodom (Gen 19; Ezek 16) as the byword for doom. Capernaum's 'you will be brought down to Hades' echoes the taunt against the king of Babylon -- 'you said, I will ascend to heaven... but you are brought down to Sheol' (Isa 14:13-15). The prophetic woe-oracle form is the vehicle. Probable.

V.5.canon_title: Thanksgiving to the Father; come to me

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Sirach 51:23-27 (Wisdom's invitation to her yoke and rest); Jeremiah 6:16 ('rest for your souls')
references.note: 'Come to me... take my yoke upon you... and you will find rest for your souls' speaks in the voice of personified Wisdom. Sirach 51:23-27 issues the same call -- draw near, 'put your neck under the yoke,' 'I have found for myself much rest' -- and 'rest for your souls' is verbatim Jeremiah 6:16. The 'yoke' also plays on the rabbinic 'yoke of Torah / of the kingdom.' Jesus offers himself as Wisdom and as the lighter yoke. Established.
scholarship: Suggs, Wisdom, Christology, and Law in Matthew

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: revelation hidden from the wise, given to the simple (cf. Dan 2; Wis 2:13-18; 10:21 LXX)
references.note: The thanksgiving that God has hidden 'these things from the wise and revealed them to infants,' with its mutual Father-Son knowledge (the so-called Johannine thunderbolt), draws on the apocalyptic-wisdom motif of revelation withheld from the clever and granted to the lowly (Dan 2; Wisdom 2:13-18). Possible as background; the saying's tradition-history is contested.

V.6.placement_flag: Grouped under 'anointings' with the Bethany anointing (Part X); likely a distinct, earlier Galilean event with a forgiveness theme.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: ancient hospitality customs (foot-washing, kiss of greeting, anointing oil); the debt-forgiveness idiom (cf. IV.6-b)
references.note: The reproach turns on the unrendered courtesies a host owed a guest -- water for the feet, a greeting-kiss, oil for the head -- which the woman supplies to excess and Simon withheld. The embedded parable of the two debtors (7:41-43) again maps sin onto DEBT and forgiveness onto release (cf. the Lord's Prayer, IV.6-b). Historical-cultural background plus the debt motif. The relationship to the Bethany anointing is flagged at the pericope level. Established.
scholarship: on the anointing traditions: Brown, AYB John, on 12:1-8

V.7.canon_title: Women who followed and supported Jesus
V.7.no_intertext: A narrative notice (Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna and others provide for the movement out of their means). It carries no citation, allusion, or identifiable tradition-trope; logged empty for comprehensive coverage rather than padded. The social datum -- women as named patrons of the movement -- belongs to the historical-cultural commentary layer, not the intertextual apparatus.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Isaiah 49:24-25 (plundering the strong one's prey); eschatological binding of the demonic prince (Isa 24:21-22; 1 En. 10; T. Levi 18)
references.note: 'No one can plunder the strong man's house unless he first binds the strong man' draws on Isaiah 49:24-25 -- can the prey be taken from the mighty? -- where God promises to contend with the captor and free the children. Behind it lies the apocalyptic hope of the binding of Belial/Satan (Isa 24:21-22; 1 Enoch 10; T. Levi 18). Jesus reads his exorcisms as the strong man already being bound. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Exodus 8:19 ('this is the finger of God')
references.note: 'If by the finger of God I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you' (Luke) alludes to Exodus 8:19, where Pharaoh's own magicians concede the plague is 'the finger of God.' The exorcisms are staged as a new exodus contest in which God's power overwhelms the opposing magic. Matthew rewrites 'finger' as 'Spirit of God' (12:28). Established; Luke's 'finger' is likely the older form.

references.speaker: other
references.source: the name Beelzebul/Beelzebub: 2 Kings 1:2-3,6 (Baal-zebub of Ekron)
references.note: The opponents' name for the demonic 'ruler' -- Beelzebul -- demonizes a foreign deity: 2 Kings 1:2-6 names Baal-zebub ('lord of flies'), god of Ekron, whom Israelite polemic deliberately distorted (Baal-zebul, 'lord of the lofty dwelling,' punned into 'lord of dung/flies'). By the first century the title had become a name for Satan. Probable historical-cultural background.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Second Temple demonology: the demon-haunted waste places (Isa 13:21; 34:14; Tobit 8:3); the unclean number seven
references.note: The expelled spirit roaming 'waterless places' seeking rest and returning with seven worse rests on the contemporary demonology in which deserts and ruins are demon-haunts (Isa 13:21; 34:14, with its Lilith and goat-demons; Tobit 8:3, where the demon flees to the Egyptian desert) and seven marks a fullness of evil. The saying trades on a shared cosmology, not a single text. Probable.
scholarship: on Second Temple demonology: Wright, The Origins of Evil Spirits

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Jonah 1:17-2:10 (Jonah in the sea-monster three days)
references.note: 'No sign except the sign of Jonah' cites Jonah, and the two evangelists DIVERGE on what the sign is. Matthew (12:40) reads it christologically: as Jonah was three days in the belly of the sea-monster, so the son of humanity will be three days in the earth -- a death-and-rising typology. Luke (11:30,32) makes Jonah's repentance-PREACHING the sign to a generation that should repent like Nineveh. Same dominical saying, two redactional interpretations -- a clean window onto how the tradition was applied. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the queen of the South (1 Kings 10:1-13) and the men of Nineveh (Jonah 3) as eschatological witnesses
references.note: The queen of Sheba who came for Solomon's wisdom (1 Kgs 10:1-13) and the Ninevites who repented at Jonah's word (Jonah 3) are summoned as witnesses who will 'rise in the judgment' and condemn the present generation -- 'something greater than Solomon / than Jonah is here.' OT figures recruited as eschatological prosecutors. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallel: Thomas 99; possible echo of Deuteronomy 33:9 (Levite covenant-loyalty over kin)
references.note: 'Whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother' redefines kinship around obedience, and is independently attested at Thomas 99 ('my mother and my brothers... those who do the will of my Father'). The redefinition faintly recalls Deuteronomy 33:9, where the loyal Levites disregard parents and kin for the covenant. Established for the Thomas parallel; the Deut echo is possible.
scholarship: DeConick, The Original Gospel of Thomas, on logion 99

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Isaiah 6:9-10 -- in the TARGUM form ('and it be forgiven them')
references.note: The parable-purpose statement cites Isaiah 6:9-10: they see but do not perceive 'lest they turn and it be forgiven them.' TEXT-FORM SHOWCASE: Mark's closing clause -- 'and it be forgiven them' (kai aphethE autois) -- matches the Aramaic TARGUM of Isaiah, not the Hebrew or LXX, which read 'and be HEALED' (kai iasomai autous). Mark is citing the synagogue Aramaic rendering. Matthew expands to the full, explicit Isaiah 6:9-10 quotation in LXX form (13:14-15), softening Mark's stark hina ('so that' they may NOT understand) toward hoti ('because'); Luke abbreviates. The theologically hardest reading -- parables that conceal in order to harden -- is Mark's, and the later evangelists ease it. Established.
scholarship: Chilton, A Galilean Rabbi and His Bible (the Targum link)
Evans, To See and Not Perceive (Isa 6:9-10 in early Judaism and the Gospels)

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallel: Gospel of Thomas 9
references.note: The parable proper is independently attested at Thomas 9 -- and crucially WITHOUT the allegorical interpretation (Mark 4:14-20). Many take the bare parable as the more primitive form, the verse-by-verse allegory (seed = word, birds = Satan, etc.) being a later interpretive overlay, since allegorization of one's own parables is uncharacteristic and the explanation's vocabulary skews to early-church mission language. Logged so the Thomas form flags where the allegory may be secondary. Established (the parallel).
scholarship: DeConick, The Original Gospel of Thomas, on logion 9
Jeremias, The Parables of Jesus (on the secondary interpretation)

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Palestinian broadcast-sowing practice (sowing before plowing)
references.note: The seed falling on the path, rocky ground, and thorns is not careless farming: in the local method the sower broadcasts seed FIRST and plows it under afterward, so seed on the trodden path and the thorn-patches is the expected wastage. The historical-cultural background corrects the modern misreading of the sower as inept and keeps the focus on the soils. Probable.
scholarship: Jeremias, The Parables of Jesus, on sowing practice

VI.2.canon_title: Lamp under a basket; the measure

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallels: Thomas 33 (lamp on a stand); Thomas 5-6 ('nothing hidden that will not be revealed'), attested in Greek at P.Oxy 654
references.note: The lamp-on-a-stand is paralleled at Thomas 33, and the maxim 'nothing is hidden that will not be revealed' at Thomas 5-6 -- the latter important because it survives in GREEK at P.Oxy 654 (lines 27-31), a witness to Thomas earlier than the Coptic and close to the Synoptic wording. Established.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 5-6, 33

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallel: Thomas 41 ('whoever has, to him will be given'); the measure-for-measure principle (cf. IV.8-a)
references.note: 'With the measure you use it will be measured to you,' and 'to the one who has, more will be given,' are paralleled at Thomas 41. The measure-clause is again the rabbinic middah k-neged middah reciprocity met at IV.8-a. Established.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on logion 41

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Joel 3:13 [MT 4:13] ('put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe'); cf. Thomas 21
references.note: The parable's close -- 'when the grain is ripe, at once he sends in the sickle, because the harvest has come' -- quotes Joel 3:13, the eschatological harvest-of-judgment image. The body of the parable stresses the seed growing 'of itself' (automatE): the kingdom comes by God's own working, not human effort, until the sudden harvest. The sickle-and-ripe-grain ending is also paralleled at Thomas 21. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the imperial world-tree with birds nesting in its branches: Ezekiel 17:23; 31:3-10; Daniel 4:10-22; cf. Thomas 20
references.note: 'The birds of the air nest in its branches/shade' deliberately invokes the OT cosmic world-tree -- the cedar sheltering all creatures as an image of empire and kingdom (Ezek 17:23; the great cedar of Ezek 31; Nebuchadnezzar's tree in Dan 4:10-22). DIVERGENCE, and it is the joke: where the prophets imagine a towering CEDAR, Jesus picks the mustard -- a fast-spreading garden SHRUB, even a weed. The kingdom-as-mighty-tree is undercut into kingdom-as-invasive-herb: it comes small, common, and uncontainable, not as imperial grandeur. Independently attested at Thomas 20. Established.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 20
Scott, Hear Then the Parable, on the mustard-seed subversion

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: leaven as a normally NEGATIVE symbol (Exod 12:15; 1 Cor 5:6-8; 'leaven of the Pharisees'); 'three measures' echoing Genesis 18:6; cf. Thomas 96
references.note: The leaven parable works by INVERSION. Leaven is otherwise a stock image of corruption and impurity -- purged at Passover (Exod 12:15), figuring malice and sin (1 Cor 5:6-8), and named as the bad influence of the Pharisees (Mark 8:15). Jesus makes this impure, hidden, fermenting agent the figure of the kingdom: it works unseen until everything is transformed. The 'three measures of flour' (an enormous batch, ~40-50 lbs) echoes the three measures Sarah bakes for the divine visitors at Mamre (Gen 18:6). Independently attested at Thomas 96. The positive use of a negative symbol is the point. Established.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 96
Scott, Hear Then the Parable, on the leaven

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallel: Thomas 57; harvest-as-judgment (Joel 3:13; cf. VI.3-a) and wheat/chaff separation (Mal 4:1; Matt 3:12)
references.note: The weeds-among-the-wheat is independently attested at Thomas 57, and -- as with the sower -- WITHOUT the allegorical interpretation that Matthew supplies (13:36-43), whose apocalyptic vocabulary (the Son of Man, the angels, the furnace of fire) is heavily Matthean-redactional. The 'let both grow till the harvest, then separate' enacts the harvest-judgment of Joel 3:13 and the wheat/chaff separation of the Baptist's winnowing (Matt 3:12; Mal 4:1). Established for the parable; the interpretation flagged as Matthean overlay.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 57

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallels: Thomas 109 (treasure hidden in a field) and Thomas 76 (the merchant and the pearl)
references.note: Both twin parables are independently attested: the hidden treasure at Thomas 109 and the merchant's pearl at Thomas 76 -- where the pearl is fused with the 'treasure in heaven that no moth devours' (cf. IV.7-a). The pair shares one logic: the single discovery worth liquidating everything to possess. Established.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 76, 109

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallel: Thomas 8 (with a DIVERGENT point); eschatological separation (cf. VI.6-a)
references.note: The dragnet that hauls in every kind of fish, sorted at the end of the age (angels separating evil from righteous), repeats the harvest-separation logic of the tares (VI.6-a). Thomas 8 has a related fishing image but makes a DIFFERENT point: a wise fisherman keeps one large fish and throws the small ones back -- choosing the one valuable thing, not end-time judgment. A case where the parallel diverges in meaning, flagged rather than harmonized; probable.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on logion 8

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: YHWH's mastery of the sea: Psalm 107:23-30; 89:9; 65:7; 104:7; the chaoskampf (Job 26:12; Ps 74:13-14; Isa 51:9-10; the Ugaritic Baal-Yamm conflict); Jonah 1
references.note: Jesus does on the lake what Scripture reserves to God. Psalm 107:23-30 is the template -- sailors in a storm cry out and 'he stilled the storm... the waves were hushed' -- with Ps 89:9, 65:7, 104:7. Behind these lies the older combat-with-the-sea (chaoskampf): God subduing Sea/Leviathan/Rahab (Job 26:12; Ps 74:13-14; Isa 51:9-10), a pattern with deep ANE roots (Baal vs. Yamm in the Ugaritic cycle). Tellingly, Jesus REBUKES (epitimaO) the wind as one rebukes a demon, treating the storm as hostile chaos.
